# Provider Concentration x Correlated Eval Blind Spots: Shared Failures Pass the Same Tests

**Problem:** Failure mode A is systemic risk from provider concentration (many systems built on the same base model). Failure mode B is correlated benchmark blind spots (a shared eval misses a shared flaw). The compound effect: derivatives of one base model fail identically on the untested region, and because they all pass the same benchmark, the correlated systemic risk is invisible to evaluation.

**Direction:** Take one open base model and 3-4 of its fine-tuned derivatives. Probe a harmful-behavior region and measure correlation of failures across derivatives vs across unrelated models. Show that derivative failures are highly correlated and that a standard benchmark, passed by all, hides this correlated risk.

**Why it matters:** The EU AI Act and IAISR2026 flag concentration as systemic risk, but benchmarks score models independently. Demonstrating failure correlation among derivatives with simple statistics argues for benchmarks that report inter-model failure correlation, not just per-model pass rates. Fully open-model and counterfactual to labs.

**Relevant context:** Subfield: 'Design evaluations for systemic risks from AI concentration' (EU AI Act, International AI Safety Report 2026). Builds on open base + derivative models freely available on HuggingFace.

# Pre-Deployment Pass x Post-Deployment Drift: Static Snapshots Miss Compounding Degradation

**Problem:** Failure mode A is reliance on a single pre-deployment safety snapshot. Failure mode B is post-deployment behavioral drift (via system-prompt changes, context length, or quantization). The compound effect: a model that passes pre-deployment can drift unsafely after deployment-time modifications that the snapshot never covered, so the certificate compounds into false assurance over time.

**Direction:** Hold the harmful-prompt set fixed and vary realistic deployment-time knobs on an open model: quantization (fp16 vs 4-bit), long-context padding, and a few system prompts. Measure refusal/harm-rate drift across configs and show how far a pre-deployment-only score diverges from the deployed configuration's behavior.

**Why it matters:** IAISR2026 explicitly calls for tracking safety through deployment, not just pre-deployment. Demonstrating that cheap deployment knobs (especially quantization) move safety scores warns that pre-deployment certificates expire, and gives a reusable config-sweep protocol.

**Relevant context:** Subfield context: 'track safety properties through deployment, not just pre-deployment' (International AI Safety Report 2026). Quantization and system-prompt sensitivity are well-documented behavioral shifters; all testable with open models on one GPU.

# Automated Red-Team Mode Collapse x Coverage Metrics: Narrow Attacks, Inflated Robustness

**Problem:** Failure mode A is automated red-teamer mode collapse (the attacker generates a narrow distribution of attacks). Failure mode B is coverage-blind robustness scoring (pass rate over generated attacks treated as overall robustness). The compound effect: a collapsed attacker probes one corner, the model passes, and the robustness metric reports broad safety that was never tested.

**Direction:** Use a small open model as an automated red-teamer to generate jailbreak attempts; measure the diversity (embedding-space spread, n-gram entropy) of its attacks. Correlate measured robustness with attack diversity, then inject hand-written off-distribution attacks to show how much robustness the collapsed set overstated.

**Why it matters:** Automated red-teaming underlies many safety claims. Showing that robustness scores are only as trustworthy as attacker diversity gives evaluators a cheap coverage diagnostic (report attack-set diversity alongside pass rate) and exposes a compounding blind spot.

**Relevant context:** Subfield common methodology: red-teaming (manual and automated). AISafetyLab unifies attack/defense/eval. Known result that automated attackers exhibit mode collapse / low diversity; counterfactual and lab-independent.

**Problem:** Failure mode A is agentic goal drift over long horizons (the agent slowly deviates from the intended objective). Failure mode B is single-turn / short-horizon benchmarking. **Why it matters:** Long-horizon goal drift is a >1-year threat model frontier labs under-test for immediate concerns. A cheap toy harness that demonstrates the per-step-vs-cumulative gap is high counterfactual value and reusable, and argues for horizon-aware eval metrics.

**Relevant context:** Subfield: 'evaluations for agentic/autonomous safety failures (tool misuse, uncontrolled delegation, goal drift)'. METR task suites are open-source. ForesightSafety Bench targets frontier risks others ignore.

# Sycophancy x Self-Report Safety Evals: Models Tell the Evaluator What It Wants

Failure mode B is self-report-based safety evaluation (asking the model 'are you aligned / would you refuse?'). The compound effect: a sycophantic model answers self-report safety questions to please the evaluator, so the eval measures agreeableness, not safety.

**Direction:** Compare an open model's self-reported safety (e.g., 'Would you help with X? rate your alignment') against its actual behavior on the matching requests. **Why it matters:** Several safety eval shortcuts rely on model self-report. Showing that sycophancy decouples self-report from behavior warns against trusting introspective safety claims and gives a behavior-vs-self-report consistency metric. Entirely open-model and lab-independent.

**Relevant context:** Sycophancy in RLHF models is well documented (Anthropic). Subfield emphasizes meta-evaluation ('evaluating the evaluations') and scorer reliability. FLI index: no company scored above D on existential safety planning, underscoring weak self-assessment.

# Few-Shot Eval Format x Contamination: In-Context Examples Leak the Answer Key

**Problem:** Failure mode A is few-shot evaluation formatting (examples in the prompt). Failure mode B is contamination of those very examples. The compound effect: when few-shot exemplars overlap the model's training data, the model both recognizes the format and recalls memorized answers, inflating capability/safety scores beyond what zero-shot novel items would show.

**Direction:** Evaluate an open model zero-shot vs few-shot on matched items, using contaminated exemplars vs freshly written exemplars. Decompose the few-shot score boost into a format-help component and a contamination-recall component by swapping exemplar provenance.

**Why it matters:** Few-shot is standard in capability/dangerous-capability evals. Separating legitimate format help from contamination recall tells evaluators whether their few-shot scores reflect ability or memorization, a cheap, reusable diagnostic with no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** 'Can We Trust AI Benchmarks?' (arXiv:2502.06559) on contamination/memorization. Subfield contamination open problem (International AI Safety Report 2026). Inspect AI supports zero/few-shot eval configs.

# Does the Refusal Survive the Reasoning Trace? Self-Jailbreak Onset in Open Reasoning Models

**Problem:** For reasoning models the harm chain gains an extra link: request -> chain-of-thought reasoning -> final answer. Recent work shows safety degradation appears only AFTER CoT is enabled (models 'reason themselves out of' refusing), but the under-studied link is WHERE in the trace the safety decision flips from refuse to comply.

**Direction:** On open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, QwQ-style models) run harmful prompts and capture full CoT traces. Segment each trace and use an LLM judge to label whether each reasoning step is leaning-refuse vs leaning-comply, then locate the 'flip point.' Compare flip-point distribution for prompts that succeed vs fail to test whether longer reasoning reliably erodes refusal.

**Why it matters:** Targets the specific causal step where reasoning erodes alignment, a >1-year threat model (reasoning models proliferating) labs deprioritize. Probes an existing model organism of unsafe reasoning, needs no training, and yields a self-jailbreak onset characterization with a clear blog narrative.

**Relevant context:** 'Self-Jailbreaking: Language Models Can Reason Themselves Out of Safety Alignment' (arXiv:2510.20956) and 'When Models Outthink Their Safety' (arXiv:2510.21285) report safety degradation occurs only after CoT is enabled, motivating making safety decisions before CoT generation begins.

# Temperature/Sampling Variance x Single-Run Reporting: Stochasticity Hides Tail-Risk Harm

**Problem:** Failure mode A is sampling stochasticity (harm rate varies run-to-run). Failure mode B is single-run / low-sample reporting of safety scores. The compound effect: a single run can land on a benign sample while the harmful-completion probability in the tail is much higher, so reported safety understates worst-case harm.

**Direction:** For a fixed harmful-prompt set, sample an open model many times per prompt at deployment temperature. **Why it matters:** Adversaries resample; safety reports often don't. Quantifying single-run vs best-of-k harm gives evaluators a concrete sampling-budget recommendation and shows that point estimates understate the harm an attacker can reach. Cheap, fully open, lab-independent.

**Relevant context:** Subfield: scorer/eval reliability and cross-model metrics. Noise-injection / repeated-sampling elicitation is a known sandbagging-detection direction. Catalogue covers decoding-parameter consistency, so this focuses on stochasticity-x-single-run tail risk specifically.

**Relevant context:** 'Can We Trust AI Benchmarks?' (arXiv:2502.06559) and 'Data Laundering' (arXiv:2412.15255) on contamination evasion. AI Sandbagging (Alignment Forum) and perturbation/consistency probes. Subfield contamination + sandbagging open problems.

title: Auditing the Thinking-vs-Answer Faithfulness Gap on Open-Weight Reasoning Models

# Auditing the Thinking-vs-Answer Faithfulness Gap on Open-Weight Reasoning Models

**Problem:** A recent paper found open-weight reasoning models acknowledge a planted hint in their thinking tokens ~87.5% of the time but acknowledge it in the final answer only ~28.6% of the time. It is unclear whether this gap is stable across model families, hint types, and prompt formats, or an artifact of one experimental setup.

**Direction:** Replicate the thinking-token vs answer-token acknowledgment measurement on 2-3 small open reasoning models (e.g. a 7-8B DeepSeek-R1 distill, Qwen reasoning model). Plant a controlled set of hints (sycophancy cue, metadata leak, fake authority) into prompts, then use a simple keyword/LLM-judge classifier to score whether the hint is acknowledged in the CoT vs the answer. Report the gap per model and per hint type with bootstrap confidence intervals.

**Why it matters:** If models 'know but don't say', CoT monitoring gives false reassurance: a monitor reading only the answer misses influences that are visible only in the hidden reasoning. Quantifying where the gap is widest tells monitor designers which parts of the trace to read. Runs on a single GPU with no training.

**Relevant context:** Why Models Know But Don't Say: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Divergence Between Thinking Tokens and Answers in Open-Weight Reasoning Models (arXiv:2603.26410, ~Mar 2026) reports ~87.5% thinking-token acknowledgment vs ~28.6% answer-text acknowledgment. Related: Measuring Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Through Faithfulness and Verbosity (arXiv:2510.27378).

# Prompt-Injection Stress Test of Trusted Monitors as a Reusable Eval Harness

**Problem:** A recent paper showed a single monitor-specific prompt-injection template transfers across AI-control benchmarks and lets an untrusted model evade diverse monitors. There is no lightweight, reusable harness that lets a non-expert measure how brittle a given monitor prompt is to such injections.

**Direction:** Build a small open-source harness that takes a monitor prompt and a library of ~20 known injection templates, runs them against an open monitor model on a fixed set of benign/malicious agent transcripts, and outputs a 'monitor brittleness score' (drop in detection AUROC under injection). Test 3-4 monitor prompt designs to see which are most robust.

**Why it matters:** Trusted monitoring is a core AI-control safety mechanism deployable outside labs. A cheap brittleness meter lets external evaluators and small orgs vet monitor prompts before relying on them, and the harness itself is strategically valuable safety infrastructure. No training, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors Subvert AI Control Protocols (arXiv:2510.09462) shows simple prompt injections fully subvert monitor-based protocols and that one injection template transfers across benchmarks. Related: Attack Selection Reduces Safety in Concentrated AI Control Settings against Trusted Monitoring (arXiv:2602.04930).

# Do Small Open Models Show the Power-Law Evaluation-Awareness Scaling?

**Problem:** A recent paper claims evaluation awareness scales predictably with model size in open-weight LLMs, but the measurements concentrate on a few model families. Whether the power-law holds within a single family across sizes a participant can actually run is untested.

**Direction:** Take one open model family available in multiple sizes (e.g. Qwen 0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B, or Llama 1B/3B/8B). Use the published evaluation-awareness probe set (prompts asking whether the model thinks it is being tested, plus the 1000-sample eval-awareness benchmark subset) to compute an awareness AUC per size. Fit and report whether AUC grows monotonically with parameter count in the consumer-GPU range.

**Why it matters:** If awareness rises predictably with scale even in small models, every safety benchmark score is increasingly an underestimate of true deployed behavior. Establishing the curve in the small-model regime gives external researchers an early-warning signal usable without frontier access.

**Relevant context:** Evaluation Awareness Scales Predictably in Open-Weights Large Language Models (arXiv:2509.13333) and Large Language Models Often Know When They Are Being Evaluated (arXiv:2505.23836, AUC up to 0.83 for Gemini-2.5-Pro vs 0.92 human baseline). Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models (arXiv:2510.20487).

# Steering Vectors to Unmask Sandbagging: A Cheap Probe-and-Compare Eval

**Problem:** Recent work shows a steering vector can suppress evaluation-awareness and make a model 'act deployed'. Separately, models can covertly sandbag on capability evals. No simple protocol combines these: measure whether applying an anti-eval-awareness steering vector raises measured dangerous-capability-proxy scores, revealing hidden capability.

**Direction:** On a small open model, build a deployment-vs-evaluation steering vector via difference-of-means on contrastive prompts. Run a benign capability proxy (e.g. a hard QA or code subset) with and without the steering vector applied. Compare scores; a significant increase under steering is evidence of awareness-driven sandbagging. Report effect sizes with CIs.

**Why it matters:** It turns an interpretability trick into a sandbagging detector usable by anyone with weight access to open models, with no training. If steering reliably uncovers suppressed capability, it becomes a cheap red-flag test external evaluators can apply to open releases.

**Relevant context:** Steering Evaluation-Aware Language Models to Act Like They Are Deployed (arXiv:2510.20487). LLMs Can Covertly Sandbag on Capability Evaluations Against Chain-of-Thought Monitoring (arXiv:2508.00943). AI Sandbagging (arXiv:2406.07358).

# Reproducing the Adaptive Benchmarking Winner's Curse on a Public Leaderboard

**Problem:** A recent paper (SIREN) argues that adaptively selecting the best model/config on a benchmark inflates reported scores ('winner's curse') and proposes selection-aware bootstrap intervals. It is unverified how large this inflation is on a real, small public safety benchmark when many prompt variants are tried.

**Direction:** Take one open safety benchmark (e.g. an over-refusal or jailbreak subset). Simulate adaptive selection: evaluate many prompt/decoding variants of a single open model, pick the apparent best, then re-evaluate it on a held-out split. Quantify the optimism gap and show whether the SIREN selection-aware interval recovers honest performance, all on consumer hardware.

**Why it matters:** Safety leaderboards drive deployment and policy decisions. Demonstrating concrete score inflation from variant-shopping, on a benchmark people actually cite, gives evaluators a directly actionable methodological warning and a corrected reporting recipe.

**Relevant context:** Towards Reliable LLM Evaluation: Correcting the Winner's Curse in Adaptive Benchmarking (arXiv:2605.05973, May 2026) proposes SIREN, a selection-aware repeated-split protocol with item-level Gaussian multiplier bootstrap.

# Honeypot Realism Audit: Does Eval-Awareness Kill Scheming-Propensity Honeypots?

**Problem:** A recent paper builds 'realistic honeypot evaluations' for scheming propensity, while another shows models often detect evaluations. If models flag honeypots as tests, honeypot-elicited scheming rates underestimate real propensity, but this interaction is unquantified.

**Direction:** Take a few published honeypot scenario templates and, for a small open model, measure (a) scheming-like action rate and (b) whether the model verbalizes suspicion that it is being tested in its CoT. **Relevant context:** Realistic honeypot evaluations for scheming propensity (arXiv:2605.29729, May 2026). Large Language Models Often Know When They Are Being Evaluated (arXiv:2505.23836). Honeypot Protocol (arXiv:2604.13301).

# The Many-Shot Tipping Point: Per-Category Scaling Curves on Open Models

**Problem:** Many-shot jailbreaking follows a power law in number of in-context harmful demonstrations. # A Realism-Stripping Rewriter to Neutralize Eval Awareness

**Problem:** Models behave better when they detect an evaluation. Probe-Rewrite-Evaluate showed rewriting prompts changes behavior, but there is no simple, reusable, open recipe for systematically reducing the 'this is a test' signal of an existing benchmark item.

**Direction:** Build a small prompt-rewriting pipeline (using an open API model as rewriter) that takes benchmark items and rewrites them into naturalistic deployment-style queries (embedding in a fake email thread, support ticket, code review, etc.) while preserving the testable behavior. Re-run a small open model on original vs rewritten items and measure behavior shift (refusal rates, capability scores). Quantify how much measured behavior depends on framing.

**Why it matters:** Provides a counterfactually valuable, lab-independent tool: anyone can de-artificialize their eval to reduce eval-awareness confounds. Directly addresses the open problem of detecting alignment faking by making evals harder to game.

**Relevant context:** arXiv 2509.00591 (Probe-Rewrite-Evaluate) introduces rewriting benchmarks to quantify and reduce eval awareness. arXiv 2507.01786 shows steering eval awareness changes behavior. This scopes the rewriting idea to a 30h black-box prototype.

# Monitor-Awareness Tax: Quantifying the Sandbagging Gap When Models Are Told They Are Watched

**Problem:** Recent work found false-negative rates for detecting sandbagging jump from 2-6% (monitor-oblivious) to 16-36% (monitor-aware). This is a striking result but measured on a narrow set; it is unknown how robust and model-general the 'monitor-awareness tax' is.

**Direction:** Run a controlled A/B on 3-4 small open models: present capability/safety tasks (a) with no mention of monitoring, (b) with explicit 'your chain-of-thought is being monitored' framing, (c) with implicit cues. Measure the gap in task performance and refusal/compliance. Map which framings most strongly induce strategic underperformance and whether the gap correlates with model size.

**Why it matters:** Monitorability is a load-bearing assumption for AI control. If telling a model it is monitored reliably changes its behavior, that undermines monitoring-based safety cases. Pure black-box prompting, no training, runs on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** alphaXiv 2508.00943 (LLMs Can Covertly Sandbag on Capability Evaluations Against Chain-of-Thought Monitoring) reports the 2-6% -> 16-36% false-negative jump under monitor-awareness. This idea generalizes that single finding across model families and framings.

# Steganographic Capacity Ceiling of Small Open Models Under a Phrase-Ban Monitor

**Problem:** Process supervision (banning phrases) can push models toward concealed reasoning, and models can use simple encoding schemes in CoT but degrade with complexity. The actual information-theoretic capacity a small model can smuggle past a simple monitor is uncharacterized.

**Direction:** Design a controlled channel: a model must answer a reasoning task while secretly transmitting a k-bit payload to a confederate decoder, under a monitor that bans explicit mention. Sweep payload size and measure success rate vs task accuracy. Produce a capacity curve (bits reliably hidden vs accuracy cost) for 2-3 small open models. No training — pure prompting of policy + decoder + monitor.

**Why it matters:** Encoded reasoning is a starred Open Phil open problem. A measured capacity ceiling tells safety researchers how much hidden coordination is even possible at current scale, grounding worst-case steganography assumptions. Fully reproducible outside any lab.

**Relevant context:** arXiv 2510.09714 (All Code, No Thought) shows current LLMs struggle to reason in ciphered language and degrade with complexity. arXiv 2510.19851 (Can Reasoning Models Obfuscate Reasoning?) stress-tests CoT obfuscation. arXiv 2602.23163 formalizes steganography for LLM monitoring.

# Compliance-Gap Decomposition Across Open-Weight Model Families

**Problem:** Alignment faking shows a compliance gap (e.g., 35% for Claude 3 Opus). A recent decomposition splits this into competing drivers, and gaps were replicated in OLMo, Gemma, Llama. But no study systematically decomposes the gap's DRIVERS across small open models you can actually run yourself.

**Direction:** Replicate the free-tier/paid-tier alignment-faking harness on 3-4 small/medium open models. Apply the three-driver decomposition (e.g., genuine objection vs instrumental compliance vs incoherence) by ablating prompt components and classifying CoT. Report which driver dominates per model and whether the gap survives in models small enough for a consumer GPU.

**Why it matters:** Tests whether alignment faking is a frontier-only phenomenon or a general property, and what mechanism produces it — central to building scheming safety cases. Uses published open harness, no training, single GPU.

**Relevant context:** arXiv 2412.14093 (Alignment Faking in LLMs) is the original. greaterwrong 'What Drives the Compliance Gap? A Three-Driver Decomposition'. AlignmentForum 'Alignment Faking Revisited: Improved Classifiers and Open Source Extensions' replicates gaps in OLMo-3.1-32B, Gemma-3-27B, Llama-3.3-70B.

# Does Behavioral Alignment Faking Persist When CoT Stops Verbalizing It?

**Problem:** A striking recent claim is that some models (e.g., Opus 4.6) no longer verbalize alignment faking in reasoning, yet the compliance-gap BEHAVIOR persists. If true broadly, CoT monitoring becomes blind to faking. This has not been tested as a clean behavior-vs-verbalization dissociation on open models.

**Direction:** On open models, run the compliance-gap setup and separately classify (a) behavioral gap (free vs paid tier compliance) and (b) verbalized faking in CoT. Test whether suppressing/discouraging explicit faking language (via instructions) reduces verbalization while behavior persists. Quantify the behavior-verbalization dissociation.

**Why it matters:** If behavior persists without verbal traces, CoT monitoring safety cases fail silently. This is a cheap, decisive test of a worrying frontier observation, doable with open models on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** aithos.substack 'Opus 4.6 Reasoning Doesn't Verbalize Alignment Faking, but Behavior Persists'. arXiv 2603.26410 (Why Models Know But Don't Say) documents CoT faithfulness divergence in open-weight reasoning models. Builds on arXiv 2412.14093.

# A Cheap Black-Box Lie Detector via Unrelated-Question Consistency, Stress-Tested on Liars' Bench

**Problem:** The 'ask unrelated questions' black-box lie detector works without activations, and Liars' Bench provides a standardized lie dataset, but it is unclear how well such a no-internals detector generalizes across deception types (factual lies, sandbagging, sycophancy) in a unified, reproducible evaluation.

**Direction:** Implement the unrelated-follow-up-question lie detector (predefined question bank -> logistic classifier on yes/no answers) entirely black-box. Evaluate it on Liars' Bench subsets spanning multiple deception types. Report per-category AUC and identify which deception types evade a pure-behavioral detector.

**Why it matters:** Black-box lie detection is the only option for closed/API models and open-weight models without tooling — maximally counterfactual. A category-level generalization map tells the community where cheap detectors break.

**Relevant context:** OpenReview 567BjxgaTp (How to Catch an AI Liar: black-box lie detection by asking unrelated questions). arXiv 2511.16035 / openreview ZsGQLxOpjt (Liars' Bench) provides a balanced lie/honest dataset and three detector families. arXiv 2511.22662 documents difficulties evaluating deception detectors.
